items.action: The term 'barca' was long used generically for any small river-traffic or fishing vessel on the Tagus.
Records list 1490 river boats, barcas and batéis, serving Lisbon, while about 1500 naus and other ships entered the port each year.

items.action: Anchored ships offshore were supplied by various types of smaller boats.

items.action: From the early 16th century, barcas began to diversify according to their functions and the routes they sailed on the Tagus.
Going upriver, entering shallow estuary channels, carrying varied cargo and fishing in river and sea required boats with differing keels, flat bottoms, bows, masts and sails.
River traffic linked the two banks, coast and interior, carrying goods and people and supporting fishing in the river and nearby coast until the mid-20th century.
Fishermen, sailors, shipwrights and caulkers built all traditional Tagus boats in wood, in shipyards mostly in riverside towns.
On the south bank, some larger shipyards operated at several towns, while others were small artisanal yards.

Varino cargo boat: elegant, decorated, keel-less, bulging hull, two bows, raked mast with lateen sail, two decks, hold with paneiros and false bulwarks for cargo.
Fragata loaded and unloaded ships anchored in Lisbon's port and goods at quays on both banks.

items.action: Fragata crews were small.
Without a favourable wind, the fragata was rowed along by a small boat usually towed behind it.
The term fragata was also commonly applied to similar-function boats such as faluas, medium-sized between bote and fragata.
From the 1860s, paddle and then propeller steamers began carrying passengers between the banks, gradually displacing small boats doing the same job.
Vila Franca de Xira bridge opened (year partly cut off in text), speeding goods transport between the banks and making upriver river navigation unprofitable for its skippers.
Frigates and varinos survived almost to the present, then nearly vanished due to ferry-boats and road freight, especially after the Tagus bridge opened.
A few botes and canoes survive in Sarilhos Pequenos and Moita thanks to enthusiasts and municipal support.
Seixal council restored old local-traffic vessels for tourism; they had served between quays and ports of the estuary until the early 1970s.
Restored boats kept by the Seixal Ecomuseum as pleasure craft: two frigate boats and one varino.

items.action: The frigate, with large sails, constant shuttling between banks and its crew's life at the quay, earned the title Queen of the Tagus Estuary; it inspired revue theatre, fados and songs.
Cacilheiros ferry people across the Tagus; the name spread because the first service linked to Cacilhas.
River links ran from Lisbon (Terreiro do Paço/Campo das Cebolas, Cais do Sodré) and Belém to Alcochete, Montijo, Barreiro, Cacilhas and Porto Brandão.
items.place: Lisbon, Belém, Alcochete, Montijo, Barreiro, Cacilhas, Porto Brandão

items.action: From early times botes, catraios and faluas linked Lisbon with Montijo, formerly Aldeia Galega or Aldegalega.
In the 19th century steamships were introduced, boats bought abroad, upriver services from Lisbon maintained, and various concessions granted.
The 20th century brought steamers purchased from several European countries and modernised mooring quays.
Two very old boats, Zagaia and Flecha, struggled across the water, with frightening crossings in the Mar da Palha in rough seas.
Some ferries also carried cars.
After 25 April things gradually improved; new or refurbished cacilheiros in the 1980s, and catamarans on Montijo–Lisbon in the mid-1990s.
Boats once left from Seixal, Montijo, Barreiro, Trafaria and Porto Brandão; many are now replaced by modern catamarans.
items.place: Seixal, Montijo, Barreiro, Trafaria, Porto Brandão

items.action: The average age of the fleet running between Cacilhas and Cais do Sodré is stated as 38 years.
Photo caption describes Cacilhas in 1970: the ferry Monte Pragal moored at one pontoon, and the ferry Setubalense arriving from Cais do Sodré at the other.
A poem, 'Cacilheiro' by Paulo Fonseca, was performed by actor José Viana in the revue Zero Zero Zé – Ordem para pagar, and published in Olisipo in 1967.
The song lyrics portray a sailor aboard an old cacilheiro, describing a moonlit crossing near the bow and the Cristo-Rei seeming to embrace Lisbon.
